newsitem.title: CHINA: China's economic performance best since 1993.
newsitem.headline: China's economic performance best since 1993.

text.p: China's Economic tsar Zhu Rongji has given a glowing account of the economy in the first eight months, saying it had given its best performance since 1993, but diplomats warned of underlying difficulties.
"There is a lot of talk that they have reached a soft landing, but I don't think they have bottomed out yet," said one Western diplomat.
All of China's macro-economic indicators basically met state targets set at the start of the year, Vice Premier Zhu told a three-day conference on cotton that closed last Thursday.
"Some are even better than expected," state media on Monday quoted him as saying.
"China's economic development has maintained steady growth in the past eight months, and the country is witnessing its best overall economic situation since 1993," Zhu said.

China's booming economy showed signs of racing out of control in 1994 and 1995, with 1994 inflation soaring to a communist-era high of 21.7 percent. Gross domestic product growth was among the highest in the world at 12.5 percent in 1994 and 10.2 percent in 1995.

China asserted macro-economic controls without sacrificing rapid and sustained economic growth and without an obvious rise in unemployment in urban areas, Zhu said, referring to a tough austerity programme and credit squeeze imposed in mid-1993.
Consumer demand had grown steadily, fixed asset investment, which roared out of control in the previous two years, had risen at sensible levels, and foreign trade had increased, he said.

Government revenues increased rapidly, while price rises had cooled. Bank deposits had swollen, despite cuts in interest rates in May and in August and the scrapping of a subsidy paid on top of normal interest to attract bank deposits.
Retail price inflation was 5.8 percent in August, and officials have said inflation could be 7.0-8.0 percent for the year, compared with a target of 10 percent.

However, the dipomat warned that inflation had been reined in by tightening the monetary screws and by cutting back lending to both the state and private sectors with little impact on economic growth, which was 9.8 percent in the first half.

"If they can maintain growth of about 10 percent, then that is really spectacular," he said, adding that he still expected the cost of the inflation battle to be reflected in economic growth. "They haven't bottomed out yet.
"They want an upbeat assessment...partly to maintain foreign investor confidence and domestic saver confidence," he said. "In a way, it is a self-fulfilling prophecy."
Zhu also described agriculture as sound, with strong early crop forecasts despite floods. Officials forecast a 480 million tonne grain harvest, up from a record 465 million last year.

But Zhu said that problems persisted among state-owned enterprises. The number of state companies losing money had risen due to outdated management systems and the production of goods that consumers did not want.

These problems had accumulated over many years and could not be solved by large investments or a relaxation of bank credits, he said, apparently responding to widespread pleas from state firm managers for more bank loans.
The two interest rate cuts had reduced interest repayments by state firms by 70 billion yuan ($8.4 billion) this year, Zhu said.

Diplomats have said the problems of state enterprises were among the most persistent of China's economic difficulties, and economists have warned that injections of funds to state firms at the expense of efficient private enterprises could create an economic slowdown over time. ($1 = 8.3 yuan)
